tip: After the 'have' word 'ganddo', the owned thing soft-mutates: 'ci' (dog) becomes 'gi' in 'mae ganddo fo gi du'.
Reported 'that... not' uses 'na' plus mutation: 'byddai' turns into 'na fyddai' (that she wouldn't) after 'addawodd hi'.
After 'â' in a command, 'p' becomes 'ph': 'poeni' turns into 'paid â phoeni' (don't worry).
'cymer' is the informal singular command 'take', from 'cymryd': 'cymer dy amser' (take your time).
'cystal' is the special 'as good as' form of 'da', used with 'â': 'cystal â'r llyfr' (as good as the book).
'Near' usually pairs with 'at', not 'i': 'yn agos at y llyfrgell' (near the library).
Welsh 'to rain' is 'bwrw glaw', literally 'to strike rain': 'bydd hi'n bwrw glaw' (it will rain).
'mor' (as/so) usually soft-mutates the next word: 'prydferth' becomes 'brydferth' in 'mor brydferth â llun' (as beautiful as a painting).
Add '-ach' for 'more' and follow with 'na' for 'than': 'yn flasusach na bwyd y caffi' (tastier than the café food).
'peidiwch â' is the plural or polite 'don't'; 'paid â' is for one person: 'peidiwch â bwydo' (don't feed).
Welsh puts the need on you: 'mae angen moddion arna i' is literally medicine is a need on me, meaning I need medicine.
'mynd yn' plus an adjective means becoming: 'mynd yn hirach' means getting longer, not simply going somewhere.
'mae'n well gen i' means I prefer, literally it is better with me, so 'mae'n well gen i gerdded' is I prefer walking.
'pa', meaning which, softens the next consonant, so 'llwybr' becomes 'lwybr' in 'pa lwybr', which path.
For a real if, Welsh uses 'os' with a future verb: 'os gorffenna i' means if I finish, then 'bydda i', I will.
'byddwn i wedi galw' means I would have called: pair it with 'pe bawn i', if I were, for the unreal past condition.
'mae'n gas gen i' means I hate, literally it is hateful with me, so 'mae'n gas gen i smocio' is I hate smoking.
The ending '-ach' usually makes comparatives, so 'anodd', hard, becomes 'anoddach', harder, in 'mae Cymraeg yn anoddach'.
Fronting a subject adds emphasis: 'y fferm sy ger y llyn' means it is the farm that is near the lake.
After 'llawer o', lots of, the next word softens, so 'pethau' becomes 'bethau' in 'llawer o bethau'.
'yn hytrach na' means rather than: 'byddai'n well gen i gerdded yn hytrach na gyrru' is I'd rather walk than drive.
To bring is 'dod â', literally come with: 'mae'r gwanwyn yn dod â'r ŵyn' means spring brings the lambs.
'pe baen nhw' means if they had, and 'bydden nhw wedi helpu' means they would have helped, the unreal past pattern.
Welsh weather uses 'bwrw', to cast: 'bwrw eira' literally casts snow and means to snow, as in 'os bydd hi'n bwrw eira'.
The object of a short-form verb normally softens, so 'pysgod', fish, becomes 'bysgod' in 'bwyton ni bysgod'.
His is 'ei', which shrinks to 'i after a vowel and softens 'crys' to 'grys' in 'smwddio'i grys', ironing his shirt.
'drwy' (through, by) softens the next word, so 'darllen' becomes 'ddarllen' in 'drwy ddarllen'.
To stress the doer, put the noun first and add 'sy'n': 'addysg sy'n agor drysau' (education is what opens doors).
'mae angen i fi' plus a verb means 'I need to' do it: 'mae angen i fi gynilo' (I need to save).
'ar gau' is the fixed phrase for 'closed' (roads, shops): 'mae'r ffordd osgoi ar gau'.
